correctness.rationale: The case split is exhaustive and direct from the defining prime-power divisibility. For odd positive \(\mu\), \(n=2\) works. For even non-powers of two, writing \(\mu=2^v m\) with odd \(m\ge3\), the choice \(n=2^{v+1}\) satisfies the sole prime-power condition and is at most \(\mu\). For \(\mu=2^v\) with composite successor, any prime divisor of \(\mu+1\) is a witness not exceeding \(\mu\). If \(2^v+1\) is prime, the standard factorization of \(x^t+1\) for odd \(t>1\) forces \(v\) itself to be a power of two. The explicit factorizations \(145=5\cdot29\) and \(627=3\cdot11\cdot19\) satisfy all required divisibilities for \(\mu=256\) and \(65536\), respectively.
risks: The finite verifier only checks sample constructions; the universal reduction is the symbolic case split above.

final_claim: For every positive \(\mu\notin\{1,2,4,16\}\), failure of the small-witness \(\mu\)-Sondow conjecture would force \(\mu=2^{2^s}\) with a new Fermat prime \(2^{2^s}+1\) for some \(s\ge5\); the two nonexcluded known Fermat-prime parameters \(256\) and \(65536\) have explicit small witnesses.
limitations: A new Fermat prime would identify a remaining shell but would not imply that the shell is a counterexample.
